```{=html}
    <section class="home-section" id="about" aria-labelledby="about-title">
      <h2 class="section__title" id="about-title">About</h2>
      <p>I am an Ezra Systems Postdoctoral Associate in Systems Engineering at Cornell University, where I work with <a href="https://www.peese.org/professor/">Professor Fengqi You</a>. I completed my Ph.D. at Shanghai Jiao Tong University in 2026, advised by <a href="https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/author/37280547200">Professor Jingcheng Wang</a>.</p>
      <p>Physical intelligence is the ability of a learning system to model a physical system and to act on it. Both parts rest on the governing dynamics of the system. I train neural networks to solve those dynamics fast enough for repeated control and optimization, and I measure how the error in a learned solution changes the decision computed from it.</p>
      <p>My current materials work concerns initiated chemical vapor deposition (iCVD) coupled with liquid crystals (LC). Chemical formation coupled with LC is a possible extension. My engineering work at Shanghai Jiao Tong University covered power generation, urban water supply, and hot-strip rolling.</p>
    </section>

    <section class="home-section" id="research" aria-labelledby="research-title">
      <h2 class="section__title" id="research-title">Research</h2>
```

{{< include _includes/research-overview.qmd >}}

```{=html}
      <ul class="directions">
        <li class="d-a"><strong>A. Physical dynamics in science and engineering.</strong> Science: iCVD coupled with liquid crystals, with Professor Fengqi You. Engineering: power generation, urban water supply, and hot-strip rolling, from my Ph.D. with Professor Jingcheng Wang.</li>
        <li class="d-b"><strong>B. Neural solvers for physical dynamics.</strong> A neural operator approximates the solution map of a governing model and returns a solution in one forward pass. I train it so that its rollouts and sensitivities are accurate enough for control and optimization.</li>
        <li class="d-c"><strong>C. Model2Action.</strong> The error in a learned solution moves the decision a little in most regimes and a lot near a critical point or an active constraint. I measure the decision error as regret, closed-loop cost, and constraint violation, and I use it to train the solver.</li>
      </ul>
      <p class="section__more"><a href="/research/">The full research program</a></p>
    </section>
```

```{=html}
    <section class="home-section" id="thinking" aria-labelledby="thinking-title">
      <h2 class="section__title" id="thinking-title">Thinking</h2>
      <p>Short notes on questions I keep returning to.</p>
      <div class="notes">
        <article class="note">
          <p class="note__meta"><time datetime="2026-09-09T18:06:06-04:00">9 September 2026, EDT (UTC−04:00)</time></p>
          <h3 class="note__title"><a href="/thinking/#from-language-to-reliable-control">Scaling and physical generalization</a></h3>
          <p>I keep wondering whether scaling can give us physical generalization. Models can share representations and solvers, but different dynamics may still require different control laws. Perhaps a model can generalize by recognizing the regime and applying local rules, without discovering a unified physical theory. What would convince me is reliable control across unfamiliar systems without extensive reference trajectories or retraining. That would suggest a general mechanism for physical reasoning.</p>
        </article>
      </div>
```
